title: The Speaker That Never Changed
voice_direction: Warm, unhurried British storyteller; quiet wonder on the 1925 reveal, a small wry smile on 'the idea wasn't new', and a soft, slowing landing on the last line.
narration: Your phone. Your earbuds. Your car. A stadium. [pause] Most of their speakers still run on an idea from nineteen twenty-five. Before that, louder meant a bigger horn. Early phonographs used no electricity at all: a needle, a diaphragm, a horn. By nineteen twenty-two, a park in California had one thirty-five feet long. Then, at General Electric, Chester Rice and Edward Kellogg tried something plainer. A coil of wire. A magnet. A paper cone. [pause] No horn at all. The odd part? The idea wasn't new. Ernst Siemens had described a coil moving in a magnet's field in eighteen seventy-four. Rice and Kellogg worked out how to make a simple cone sound right, and built an amplifier strong enough to drive it. In nineteen twenty-six, RCA sold it as the Radiola one-oh-four, amplifier built in. Then everything around it changed. In nineteen thirty-one, Alan Blumlein filed a patent for sound in two channels, left and right. Stereo. In nineteen seventy-nine, Sony's Walkman put music in your ears, on the move. Then the iPod. Then the wires vanished. But open almost any of them up. [pause] A coil. A magnet. A cone, pushing air. [softly] The music changed completely. The speaker, hardly at all.

instagram_caption:
Before 1925, if you wanted sound to be louder, you needed a bigger horn. Early phonographs used no electricity at all: a needle, a diaphragm, a horn. By 1922 a park in California had a horn 35 feet long.

Then, at General Electric in Schenectady, Chester Rice and Edward Kellogg tried something plainer: a coil of wire, a magnet and a paper cone. No horn at all.

The odd part is that the idea wasn't new. Ernst Siemens had described a coil moving in a magnet's field in 1874. What Rice and Kellogg worked out was how to make a simple cone sound right, and an amplifier strong enough to drive it. RCA sold it in 1926 as the Radiola 104, amplifier built in.

Then everything around the speaker changed: stereo (Alan Blumlein's patent, filed 14 December 1931), the Walkman (1 July 1979), the iPod (2001), wireless earbuds. Open almost any of them up and you'll find the same three things: a coil, a magnet, a cone pushing air.

What's the oldest thing you still play music on? 👇

facts.claim: The moving-coil (electrodynamic) driver is the most common type of loudspeaker driver; invented in its modern form by Kellogg and Rice in 1925
facts.source: Wikipedia, 'Electrodynamic speaker driver' and 'Loudspeaker' (read via search, not fetched)

facts.claim: Today's most widely used speakers keep the basic shape and parameters Rice and Kellogg described; magnets and materials changed
Acoustic phonographs and gramophones played back with no electricity: stylus, diaphragm, horn
facts.source: Library of Congress, 'History of the Cylinder Phonograph' (well established; not re-fetched this session)

facts.claim: Edison photographed with his tinfoil phonograph, Washington, 18 April 1878
facts.source: Library of Congress, Brady-Handy Collection record

facts.claim: 1922: a Magnavox horn about 35 ft long, spruce, 12 ft square mouth, at Idora Park, California
facts.source: Commons file description citing Electrical Record, 1922

facts.claim: Chester W. Rice and Edward W. Kellogg, General Electric, Schenectady: hornless moving-coil cone loudspeaker; paper presented at the AIEE Spring Convention, St. Louis, 13–17 April 1925, published Journal of the A.I.E.E. vol. 44 no. 9, Sept 1925
facts.source: AES historical pages (Rice-Kellogg); ARSCList citation of the paper footnote; IEEE Xplore (DOI 10.1109/JAIEE.1925.6534260)

facts.claim: Ernst W. Siemens was the first to describe the moving-coil transducer: a circular coil in a magnetic field, free to move axially (US patent 149,797, 1874)
The Rice–Kellogg work included an amplifier design that boosted the power delivered to the loudspeaker
RCA Radiola Loudspeaker 104 went on sale in 1926: a dynamic (field-coil) speaker with an integrated power amplifier and mains supply
facts.source: Radiomuseum.org RCA 104 entry; Commons description of the 1925 Kellogg–Rice photo

facts.claim: Alan Blumlein's British patent 394,325 (two-channel 'binaural' sound, i.e. stereo): applied for 14 December 1931, accepted 14 June 1933, filed by EMI
facts.source: Wikipedia 'United Kingdom patent 394325'; antiquarian listing of the printed patent (application no. 34,657/31)

facts.claim: Sony Walkman TPS-L2 went on sale in Japan on 1 July 1979 (¥33,000)
facts.source: South China Morning Post / AFP, Walkman 40th anniversary; Walkman Archive
